newsitem.title: USA: Latam regulators urged to monitor interbank rates.
newsitem.headline: Latam regulators urged to monitor interbank rates.

text.p: Latin American regulators should closely monitor telltale domestic interest rates that can serve as early warning signs to help prevent financial crises, Inter-American Development Bank (IADB) experts advised on Friday.
At a conference on the fringes of the IMF-World Bank annual meeting, IADB economists also recommended policies to strengthen banks in a region known for colossal financial catastrophes.

The cleanup of last year's Mexico's banking crisis has already cost that country the equivalent of six percentage points of GDP. Venezuela's 1994 collapse consumed a full 15 percentage points of its GDP.
IADB principal advisor Liliana Rojas-Suarez and bank consultant Steven Weisbrod suggested that Latin American regulators keep close tabs on their interbank markets.
Pointing to their research on Argentina and Mexico, the economists said regulators could have divined which banks would get into trouble as early as two years before the 1995 peso crisis.
"Many of the banks that paid the highest rates in the interbank markets in 1993 and 1994 were the ones that had to be rescued last year," said Rojas-Suarez.
She also argued that that risk-weighted capital-to-assets banking standards were not as effective in Latin America as in industrialized countries.

In many Latin American countries, where wealth is highly concentrated, banks are often the financial arms of large business groups. Loose accounting standards allow bank owners to shuffle assets between their holdings to produce picture-perfect balance sheets for regulators.
Domestic interbank markets usually had the knack of telling who was headed for trouble, Rojas-Suarez said.
Ecuador's Central Bank general manager, Augusto de la Torre, acknowledged that the quality of bank capital in the region could be fictitious.
He recounted the case of an Ecuadorean bank that transfered deposits through a web of offshore corporations, only to repatriate the funds as genuine capital increases.
"We know that good capital only grows through sweat and tears, so quick capital expansion usually puts banks on the list of suspects," he said.
The IADB's chief economist, Ricardo Hausmann, said Latin American countries should actively promote foreign investment in their banking industry, just as they do in other sectors of their economies.
"Latin America is integrated to international financial markets but its links are shallow. There's where the dangers lie," he said.
Hausmann pointed out that the opening of capital accounts in Latin America have not translated into cheaper, better or more varied financial products for consumers.

With the exception of Panama, which has a highly developed domestic banking sector besides its well-known offshore financial services industry, in most Latin American countries bank debt represents a relatively low percentage of GDP.
According to Hausmann, opening up Latin American financial markets to foreign banks and encouraging domestic banks to turn international will promote stability in two ways.

On one hand, foreign banks will have access to their parents' stock of capital and international liquidity if they get in trouble. On the other, regionally diversified banks will be more likely to weather country-specific shocks.
